summary: A status report on an experiment in letting users on different ARPANET hosts talk to each other from their terminals, ask who is online, and perhaps share programs. It grows out of a 1971 Network Working Group discussion of inter-entity communication. The RFC describes the experiment, not a finished protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 441 reports on an experiment that lets people on different networked computers find and contact one another. It describes commands and an interim protocol, while inviting more experimentation.

questions: how did early arpanet users chat
subtitle: A status report on an experiment in communication across network hosts.

tldr.problem: Users wanted to find other users and communicate across different hosts, not just within one time-sharing system.
tldr.mechanism: The experiment uses server and user programs, commands for finding users and linking terminals, and an interim protocol for requests.
tldr.outcome: The RFC reports an operational experiment and invites further participation; it does not define a finished standard.

sections.title: Communication Across Hosts
sections.content:
RFC 441 reports on an experiment in inter-entity communication (IEC). It explores extending familiar time-sharing functions, such as finding users and linking terminals, across host boundaries on the network.

The authors describe development as ad hoc and the protocol as an interim design. The report covers implementations at MIT-DMCG and through the TENEX RSEXEC subsystem.
sections.plainLanguage: The experiment extends ways to find users and connect terminals from one computer to other network hosts. The RFC describes early implementations, not a final protocol.

sections.title: Ports and Terminal Connections
sections.content:
The MIT user program represents streams entering and leaving an object with ports. A user can open or close ports to control connections among a terminal, a job, and consultants; the RFC's diagram shows these parts connected through separate input and output ports.

This design lets the user choose which streams are connected during a conversation. The note says ports can be controlled individually.
sections.plainLanguage: Ports represent separate input and output streams. Users can open or close them to choose which terminals or jobs communicate.

sections.title: Commands and the Interim Protocol
sections.content:
The MIT interface includes WHO, WHERE, OPEN, CLOSE, PORT MAP, CONNECT, and DISCONNECT. RSEXEC offers related cross-host functions, including commands to locate users, list sites, and link terminals.

The RFC also describes an initial connection followed by commands such as USINF, SSTAT, and LINK. It assigns socket 245 decimal to the experiment and invites sites to participate.
sections.plainLanguage: Commands can list users, search for a user, or establish and end a terminal link. The RFC gives the message exchange used by the interim RSEXEC protocol.
